I understand and generally agree with the jist of this article but there's are some very weighty counterpointa that the author did not mention.

Routine medical costs

It's true that this is mot the sort of thing that insurance is typically meant to cover, but this is also a preventative value to the routine stuff that lowers the overall costs because people will get vaccines and not get sick, or their illnesses will get caught earlier and will be less expensive to treat as a result. If routine stuff is not covered then those costs are a disincentive to actually getting routine treatments and the people who dont get that routine stuff will be more expensive when the coverage kicks in because they got really sick. The cost factor is so significant that many plans incentivize thhe routine shit even further by offering a premium discount or extra money in the hsa if you get routjne checkups.

Preexisting conditions

Since so many expensive conditions can not be limited to a single policy period or particular plan, there has to be some kind of regulation addressing this. Since it is a competitive disadvantage for any insurer to cover preexisting conditions when they are not required to, any insurer that covered them would be flooded with the unprofitable policies for people with preexisting conditions and would soon be bankrupt. The idea behind prohibiting insurers from refusing to cover preexisting conditions is that then the unprofitable policies would be randomly distributed throughout the carriers and no carrier would be more disadvantaged by them than another. The idea is generally sound but has kinks in practice. Insurers greatest fear is that people will just sit out insurance markets altogether until they get sick and now the insurance co is on the hook for the bill for someone who had never paid more in premiums than they received in benefits. That's the fear that was behind the Obamacare mandate. It is not an unreasonable fear and I don't know what the best solution is. I don't think we can go back to how it was when insurers had to pick and choose the illnesses that they would be willing to cover in order to provide a competitive insurance quote. That is a recipe for a different type of moral hazard, and the govt will be stuck with the bill anyway if someone waives heart attack coverage then gets one, for example.
